items.article: BRO’s Shyok road plan could give India an additional access route towards DBO and Depsang, strengthening logistics and providing an alternative link along the China border. India is drawing up plans for another major road corridor in strategically sensitive eastern Ladakh, with the Border Roads Organisation (BRO) moving to prepare a Detailed Project Report for a 150-km road along the eastern bank of the Shyok River towards Daulat Beg Oldi. The proposed road will run for 150 km and has been divided into five packages. The project is part of the Darbuk-Shyok-Daulat Beg Oldi road network and is proposed to be developed to NHDL specifications. The location of the proposed road gives the project considerable strategic significance. Daulat Beg Oldi, or DBO, is located in the Sub-Sector North of eastern Ladakh, close to the Line of Actual Control (LAC) with China. The area includes the strategically important Depsang Plains and lies close to the Karakoram Pass. The existing Darbuk-Shyok-Daulat Beg Oldi road has already transformed India’s ability to move personnel and supplies towards the northernmost areas of Ladakh. A new alignment along the eastern bank of the Shyok could provide additional road capacity and, potentially, an alternative route in a region where logistics and mobility are critical. The biggest advantage could be redundancy.

items.article: An Interpol executive warns AI is making existing cyber threats faster and harder to detect, while companies face new risks from the rise of agentic AI. Artificial intelligence enables cyber threats by enhancing existing criminal tactics such as scams and fraud, according to Interpol. AI is enhancing existing criminal techniques rather than revolutionizing them, Bjorn R. Watne, global chief information security officer at Interpol, told CNBC on the sidelines of Tech Week Singapore on Thursday. Scam operators can use AI to target multiple victims simultaneously, while improved translation and digital identities are making it increasingly difficult to distinguish fraudulent interactions from real ones. "It's an evolution and not a revolution," Watne said, adding that AI is primarily increasing the "speed and scale" of existing techniques. As cyber threats evolve, companies should prioritize protective actions, according to Watne. Instead, businesses should first identify their "crown jewels," the assets most critical to keeping their operations running, and determine who would be most interested in stealing or disrupting them. They can then use threat intelligence to understand the tactics and technologies used by those adversaries and tailor their defenses accordingly.

The H-1B programme allows US employers to hire foreign workers for specialised occupations, including jobs in technology, engineering and healthcare. But a paper published in JAMA Internal Medicine suggests that another factor plays a bigger role in maintaining a sex life as you age than “sexual function”. Among those in midlife or older age, the study found that the “importance” of sex matters. The researchers used data from a group of women who took part in the Do Stage Transitions Result in Detectable Effects (STRIDE) program. This is a cohort study of women who enrolled in 2005, when they were aged between 40 and 65. Starting in year four of the study, participants began answering questionnaires about their sexual function and how important they deemed sex. They also shared information designed to gauge their hormonal state and whether they were sexually active.

The award recognises his decades of work linking geometry, topology, dynamics and probability. Mahan Mj gave up research mathematics for six years to become a monk. When he returned, almost by accident, he answered a question that had stood since the early 1980s. In early 1998, a freshly minted Berkeley PhD walked away from research mathematics. Mahan Mj, who had just finished a doctorate on a problem about chaos and symmetry, had decided to become a monk of the Ramakrishna Order. For the next six years, he did no research mathematics at all. The problem he would later solve is, at heart, a question about order and disorder. Picture a globe being pushed and turned in infinitely many ways at once. Somewhere on its surface, the motion becomes wildly unpredictable, and mathematicians wanted to know whether that chaos could be mapped and tamed. In 2004, the Internet gave him a reason to look back. Out of what he calls "moderately idle curiosity," he searched for work done in his absence and found two new papers by Bowditch and McMullen. He set out to reprove and generalise them using the framework from his thesis. New ideas began to emerge, and they eventually led to a solution of a problem posed by William Thurston in the early 1980s. items.text: What is weaponised pooping? Your partner could be doing it too
items.article: A fresh internet debate has framed long bathroom breaks as a way to dodge chores and family responsibilities. The term has prompted humour, frustration and wider discussion around domestic labour and health risks. Does it ever happen that you are in the middle of a heated argument with your partner and, suddenly, they say they need to go to the washroom? They do so — and then spend what feels like an eternity in there. Or perhaps your mother asks your sibling to make tea, only for them to suddenly announce that they have to answer nature’s call. The call, mysteriously, doesn't seem to end until the tea is ready — and perhaps even gulped down. The internet has a term for it: weaponised pooping. Before you let your imagination run wild, there is no diarrhoea or aggressive pooping involved. The "weapon" here is simply the bathroom break itself, which becomes a convenient escape hatch from responsibilities, household chores, confrontation and, sometimes, the general chaos happening outside the bathroom door. Weaponised pooping, explained The idea is fairly simple. Someone walks into the bathroom because they genuinely need to go. Fair enough. But then the phone comes out. One reel becomes five. A little doomscrolling turns into a rabbit hole. Suddenly, 10 minutes have become 40. But sometimes, the timing is suspiciously convenient.
